hints: Think about what the word inducible means in everyday language - something is switched on by a trigger rather than being on all the time. What could the trigger be here?
Link that trigger to saving energy - why would a bacterium avoid making lactose-digesting enzymes when only glucose is available, and what must happen at the DNA level when lactose appears?
walkthrough:
What Inducible Really Means**
Think of inducible as made on demand. E. coli prefers glucose because it is easier to respire. Making enzymes to digest lactose all the time would waste amino acids, ATP and ribosome time, so the cell keeps those genes off until they are needed.

How Switching On Happens**
When lactose is present, lactose (as allolactose) acts as an inducer. It binds to the repressor protein, so the structural genes for lactose metabolism are expressed / transcribed only at that time. That on-demand production is exactly why they are called inducible enzymes.

Final answer: Enzymes are only produced when lactose / allolactose / substrate is present, when required. Structural genes are not transcribed continuously, but are switched on when lactose / allolactose binds to the repressor.

hints: Start with the graph at 0 min - activity is near zero then rises steeply to about 0.8 by 60 min. What has just changed in the medium to start this rise?
Recall what normally blocks the lac operon when lactose is absent. What protein sits on the DNA and where does it sit?
Think about what happens when that blocking protein meets lactose - how does its shape and its grip on DNA change?
Once the block is removed, what enzyme can now access the DNA and what process does it start to make beta-galactosidase?
Connect more enzyme molecules being made over time to the steep rise in activity, and remember what beta-galactosidase actually does to lactose.
Look at the end of the curve from about 120 to 200 min - activity plateaus at 1.0 arbitrary units. What does a flat line tell you about the rate of new active enzyme appearing?
For that plateau, think about limits - when every gene is fully switched on or every enzyme active site is occupied, can activity keep rising forever?
walkthrough:
Setting The Scene At 0 Minutes**
At 0 min glucose is gone and excess lactose is added. Activity is about 0.0, because with no lactose before this the operon was repressed and almost no beta-galactosidase was present. Lactose now enters the bacterial cells.

Removing The Brake**
Without lactose, repressor protein is bound to the operator DNA and physically blocks transcription. Lactose (as allolactose) binds to the repressor and changes its tertiary shape, so it can no longer fit the operator. The repressor falls off and the promoter region is unblocked.

Switching Transcription On**
With the operator free, RNA polymerase can bind to the promoter and transcribe the structural genes (lacZ) into mRNA. Ribosomes then translate this mRNA, so new beta-galactosidase molecules are made. That is why the curve climbs steeply from 20 to 80 min, reaching about 0.9 arbitrary units by 100 min.

Why Activity Rises And Then Plateaus**
Each new beta-galactosidase molecule can hydrolyse lactose to glucose and galactose, so measured activity rises as enzyme concentration rises. After about 120-150 min the curve flattens at 1.0 arbitrary units. The operon is now fully induced and enzyme production balances loss, so maximum activity is reached and active sites are effectively saturated - no further increase is possible.

Final answer: Lactose enters bacterium and binds to repressor, causing shape change so repressor detaches from operator, unblocking promoter. RNA polymerase binds to promoter and structural gene(s) are transcribed, so beta-galactosidase is made which breaks down lactose. Activity rises then levels off at maximum as all genes fully expressed / active sites full.
